reason: The run renders the Jewish-expert sense as "scribe" in 60 verses but departs to "scholar" at 1 Corinthians 1:20, where its own note identifies the same sense. Modern translations also split on this word ("scribe", "teacher of the law", "legal expert"), so drift is likely without an entry. Acts 19:35 is a separate civic sense and is correctly rendered differently.
sense: Jewish expert in the Law of Moses and the Scriptures, who taught and interpreted them

alternates.when: The chief civic official of a Greek city, a different sense of the word. Only at Acts 19:35 (Ephesus).

rationale: "Scribe" can suggest a mere copyist to a modern reader, but it is still the recognised English term for this Jewish class of Scripture experts, and no replacement is clearly better. "Teacher of the law" is a gloss rather than a title, and "scholar" or "lawyer" brings in modern associations. A background note can explain the role, so the traditional word is kept everywhere the Jewish expert is meant. That includes 1 Corinthians 1:20, where Paul most likely sets the Jewish Scripture expert beside the sage and the debater.
standard_view: KJV, RSV, NRSV, ESV, NASB and most scholarly literature use "scribe" in the Gospels and Acts. NIV has "teacher of the law", CEB "legal expert", and NET "expert in the law". At 1 Corinthians 1:20 most keep "scribe", though NIV has "teacher of the law" and some recent versions have "scholar"; a minority of interpreters take the word there more generally as a learned person. At Acts 19:35 virtually all versions have "town clerk" or "city clerk".
